claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn is initially an FCC solid solution.
The initial FeNiCrMn structure contains pre-existing chemical short-range-order clusters.
The initial structure is free of vacancy clusters and twin boundaries.
FeNiCrMn yield stress remains constant from 10^8 to 10^10 s^-1.
FeNiCrMn yield stress decreases monotonically with increasing temperature.
Thermal vibrations reduce the critical resolved shear stress.
Plastic deformation is initiated by Shockley partial dislocations on {111} planes.
Twinning and FCC-to-BCC transformation are absent under the stated conditions.
SRO clusters act as local friction barriers to dislocation motion.
SRO clusters serve as nucleation sites for Shockley partial dislocations.
Shockley partials nucleate by thermally activated overcoming of SRO-induced barriers produced by local lattice distortion.
Overcoming SRO-induced friction, rather than vacancy diffusion or vacancy-cluster availability, is the rate-limiting nucleation step.
SRO-controlled nucleation explains the strain-rate insensitivity of yield strength.
Yield stress is orientation-dependent because crystallographic orientation changes activation of Shockley partials on {111} planes.
The <11-1> orientation has a higher maximum yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The <11-1> loading direction maximizes resolved shear stress on the active {111} plane relative to <110>.
The HCP-like regions are intrinsic stacking faults bounded by Shockley partials rather than a transformed phase.
The HCP-like regions will disappear upon unloading or annealing.
Disappearance of the HCP-like regions will occur without a change in local chemical composition.
Significant strain-rate dependence in the SRO-free system, while the SRO-containing system remains insensitive, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The explanation says <11-1> maximizes resolved shear stress relative to <110> but then uses that fact to predict that a higher macroscopic stress is required. For a fixed critical resolved shear stress, a larger resolved-shear factor would ordinarily imply a lower required macroscopic stress; no additional orientation-dependent barrier is quantified to resolve this internal mismatch.

The central hypothesis attributes rate insensitivity to SRO, yet the stated rule says that observing rate dependence after removing SRO while retaining insensitivity with SRO would falsify the hypothesis. That result would instead support the proposed causal role of SRO.
